explain.say: Tyger Tyger, burning bright. William Blake printed that line in 1794, and readers are still arguing about it. Close reading means reading slowly, as if every word was chosen on purpose, because it was. The chain on the board shows the five moves you will make.

explain.say: Move one: notice. Read the poem twice, aloud. See how the word splits on the board? TY-ger, with the beat falling first, like a hammer hitting an anvil. And Blake spells it with a y, which makes it strange and old. Which word would you underline first?

draw.name: x-word
draw.note: Stress on the first beat: TY-ger, a hammer blow

explain.say: Now sort what you noticed. Look at the three groups. Sounds that pound, images from a blacksmith's forge, like the furnace and the anvil, and question after question. In fact the whole poem is questions with no answers. What kind of maker uses a hammer and chains?

draw.name: x-sort
draw.question: What do you notice in The Tyger?

explain.say: Here is the key detail. The first stanza asks what hand could frame thy fearful symmetry. The last stanza repeats it, but could becomes dare. See the glowing Interpret step? One word moves the poem from wonder at the maker's skill to awe at the maker's nerve.

explain.say: Last move: argue. Write a claim, quote a word or two, then explain the effect. For example: the change from could to dare turns admiration into fear. Lovely work. Exam tip: a single well-chosen word beats a long quotation. Challenge: find one word that changes in a poem you are studying.

faq.a: Close reading is slow, careful attention to the words of a short passage: their sounds, images, patterns and shifts, and what those choices do to meaning.

faq.q: How do I start close reading a poem?
faq.a: Read it twice, aloud. Underline anything that surprises you: an odd word, a repeated sound, a change of tone. Then ask why it is there.
asks: Where do I begin with a poem?

faq.q: What changes between the first and last stanza of The Tyger?
faq.a: Almost nothing, except one word. Could frame becomes dare frame, so the question moves from whether a maker was able to create the tiger to whether a maker would dare to.
asks: Why does Blake repeat the first stanza?

faq.q: How do I turn notes into an argument?
faq.a: Make a claim about meaning, support it with a short quotation, then analyse the exact words. Link each paragraph back to your main argument.
asks: How do I write a close reading essay?

faq.q: Why is Tyger spelled with a y?
faq.a: Spelling was looser in the 1790s, and Blake chose the older form. Today the y makes the animal feel strange, ancient and almost mythical.
asks: Why does Blake spell tiger as Tyger?

facts: The Tyger appeared in Blake's Songs of Experience in 1794.
Blake printed his poems himself by relief etching on copper and coloured many copies by hand.
The Tyger is paired with The Lamb from Songs of Innocence, published in 1789.

quiz.why: What immortal hand or eye dare frame thy fearful symmetry: dare replaces could.

wrong.0: The verb frame stays the same; the change is in could.
wrong.2: Blake uses dare, which adds courage or nerve.
